entries.d83192425e284f8cc741c0a0d59f8ba066ba12c9: <div sID="gen10687" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="Ps.20" sID="Ps.20"/> <div eID="gen10687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10688" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10689" type="x-p"/> It is the will of God that prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings, should be made, in special manner, for kings and all in authority. This psalm is a prayer, and the next a thanksgiving, for the king. David was a martial prince, much in war. Either this psalm was penned upon occasion of some particular expedition of his, or, in general, as a form to be used in the daily service of the church for him. In this psalm we may observe, I. What it is they beg of God for the king, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. With what assurance they beg it. The people triumph (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.5">ver. 5</reference>), the prince (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">ver. 6</reference>), both together (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7-Ps.20.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), and so he concludes with a prayer to God for audience, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">ver. 9</reference>. In this, David may well be looked upon as a type of Christ, to whose kingdom and its interests among men the church was, in every age, a hearty well-wisher.
entries.171d9d567841c271d4805e119dd54790a57acb0e: <div eID="gen10689" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10688" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Petitions against Sin.</title> <div sID="gen10690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hear thee in the day of trouble; the name of the God of Jacob defend thee; <hi type="super">2</hi> Send thee help from the sanctuary, and strengthen thee out of Zion; <hi type="super">3</hi> Remember all thy offerings, and accept thy burnt sacrifice; Selah. <hi type="super">4</hi> Grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfil all thy counsel. <hi type="super">5</hi> We will rejoice in thy salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up <hi type="italic">our</hi> banners: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> fulfil all thy petitions. <div eID="gen10690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10691" type="x-p"/> This prayer for David is entitled <hi type="italic">a psalm of David;</hi> nor was it any absurdity at all for him who was divinely inspired to draw up a directory, or form of prayer, to be used in the congregation for himself and those in authority under him; nay it is very proper for those who desire the prayers of their friends to tell them particularly what they would have to be asked of God for them. Note, Even great and good men, and those that know ever so well how to pray for themselves, must not despise, but earnestly desire, the prayers of others for them, even those that are their inferiors in all respects. Paul often begged of his friends to pray for him. Magistrates and those in power ought to esteem and encourage praying people, to reckon them their strength (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.5">Zech. xii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">10</reference>), and to do what they can for them, that they may have an interest in their prayers and may do nothing to forfeit it. Now observe here, <div eID="gen10691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10692" type="x-p"/> I. What it is that they are taught to ask of God for the king. <div eID="gen10692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10693" type="x-p"/> 1. That God would answer his prayers: <hi type="italic">The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">v. 1</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the Lord fulfil all thy petitions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.20.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, (1.) Even the greatest of men may be much in trouble. It was often a day of trouble with David himself, of disappointment and distress, of treading down and of perplexity. Neither the crown on his head nor the grace in his heart would exempt him from the trouble. (2.) Even the greatest of men must be much in prayer. David, though a man of business, a man of war, was constant to his devotions; though he had prophets, and priests, and many good people among his subjects, to pray for him, he did not think that excused him from praying for himself. Let none expect benefit by the prayers of the church, or of their ministers or friends for them, who are capable of praying for themselves, and yet neglect it. The prayers of others for us must be desired, not to supersede, but to second, our own for ourselves. Happy the people that have praying princes, to whose prayers they may thus say, <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> <div eID="gen10693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10694" type="x-p"/> 2. That God would protect his person, and preserve his life, in the perils of war: "<hi type="italic">The name of the God of Jacob defend thee,</hi> and set thee out of the reach of thy enemies." (1.) "Let God by his providence keep thee safe, even the God who preserved Jacob in the days of his trouble." David had mighty men for his guards, but he commits himself, and his people commit him, to the care of the almighty God. (2.) "Let God by his grace keep thee easy from the fear of evil.—<reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">The name of the Lord is a strong tower, into which the righteous run</hi> by faith, <hi type="italic">and are safe;</hi> let David be enabled to shelter himself in that strong tower, as he has done many a time." <div eID="gen10694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10695" type="x-p"/> 3. That God would enable him to go on in his undertakings for the public good—that, in the day of battle, he would <hi type="italic">send him help out of the sanctuary, and strength out of Zion,</hi> not from common providence, but from the ark of the covenant and the peculiar favour God bears to his chosen people Israel. That he would help him, in performance of the promises and in answer to the prayers made in the sanctuary. Mercies out of the sanctuary are the sweetest mercies, such as are the tokens of God's peculiar love, the blessing of God, even our own God. Strength out of Zion is spiritual strength, strength in the soul, in the inward man, and that is what we should most desire both for ourselves and others in services and sufferings. <div eID="gen10695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10696" type="x-p"/> 4. That God would testify his gracious acceptance of the sacrifices he offered with his prayers, according to the law of that time, before he went out on a dangerous expedition: <hi type="italic">The Lord remember all thy offerings and accept thy burnt-sacrifices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">v. 3</reference>), or <hi type="italic">turn them to ashes;</hi> that is, "The Lord give thee the victory and success which thou didst by prayer with sacrifices ask of him, and thereby give as full proof of his acceptance of the sacrifice as ever he did by kindling it with fire from heaven." By this we may now know that God accepts our spiritual sacrifices, if by his Spirit he kindles in our souls a holy fire of pious and divine affection and with that makes our hearts burn within us. <div eID="gen10696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10697" type="x-p"/> 5. That God would crown all his enterprises and noble designs for the public welfare with the desired success (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord grant thee according to thy own heart.</hi> This they might in faith pray for, because they knew David was a man after God's own heart, and would design nothing but what was pleasing to him. Those who make it their business to glorify God may expect that God will, in one way or other, gratify them: and those who walk in his counsel may promise themselves that he will fulfil theirs. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt devise a thing and it shall be established unto thee.</hi> <div eID="gen10697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10698" type="x-p"/> II. What confidence they had of an answer of peace to these petitions for themselves and their good king (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We will rejoice in thy salvation.</hi> We that are subjects will rejoice in the preservation and prosperity of our prince;" or, rather, "In thy salvation, O God! in thy power and promise to save, will we rejoice; that is it which we depend upon now, and which, in the issue, we shall have occasion greatly to rejoice in." Those that have their eye still upon the salvation of the Lord shall have their hearts filled with the joy of that salvation: <hi type="italic">In the name of our God will we set up our banners.</hi> 1. "We will wage war in his name; we will see that our cause be good and make his glory our end in every expedition; we will ask counsel at his mouth, and take him along with us; we will follow his direction, implore his aid and depend upon it, and refer the issue to him." David went against Goliath in the name of the Lord of hosts, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45">1 Sam. xvii. 45</reference>. (2.) "We will celebrate our victories in his name. When we lift up our banners in triumph, and set up our trophies, it shall be in the name of our God; he shall have all the glory of our success, and no instrument shall have any part of the honour that is due to him." <div eID="gen10698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10699" type="x-p"/> In singing this we ought to offer up to God our hearty good wishes to the good government we are under and to the prosperity of it. But we may look further; these prayers for David are prophecies concerning Christ the Son of David, and in him they were abundantly answered; he undertook the work of our redemption, and made war upon the powers of darkness. In the day of trouble, when his soul was exceedingly sorrowful, the Lord heard him, heard him in that he feared (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">sent him help out of the sanctuary,</hi> sent an angel from heaven to strengthen him, took cognizance of his offering when he made his soul an offering for sin, and accepted his burnt-sacrifice, turned it to ashes, the fire that should have fastened upon the sinner fastening upon the sacrifice, with which God was well pleased. And he granted him according to his own heart, made him to see of the travail of his soul, to his satisfaction, prospered his good pleasure in his hand, fulfilled all his petitions for himself and us; for him the Father heareth always and his intercession is ever prevailing.
entries.54716b71c8038817a72f19fb16cf5d1f05c32bd8: <div eID="gen10699" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Subject's Prayer for the Sovereign.</title> <div sID="gen10700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Now know I that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saveth his anointed; he will hear him from his holy heaven with the saving strength of his right hand. <hi type="super">7</hi> Some <hi type="italic">trust</hi> in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <hi type="super">8</hi> They are brought down and fallen: but we are risen, and stand upright. <hi type="super">9</hi> Save, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : let the king hear us when we call. <div eID="gen10700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10701" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Holy David himself triumphing in the interest he had in the prayers of good people (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now know I</hi> (I that pen the psalm know it) <hi type="italic">that the Lord saveth his anointed,</hi> because he hath stirred up the hearts of the seed of Jacob to pray for him." Note, It bodes well to any prince and people, and may justly be taken as a happy presage, when God pours upon them a spirit of prayer. If he see us seeking him, he will be found of us; if he cause us to hope in his word, he will establish his word to us. Now that so many who have an interest in heaven are praying for him he doubts not but that God will hear him, and grant him an answer of peace, which will, 1. Take its rise from above: <hi type="italic">He will hear him from his holy heaven,</hi> of which the sanctuary was a type (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">Heb. ix. 23</reference>), from the throne he hath prepared in heaven, of which the mercy-seat was a type. 2. It shall take its effect here below: He will hear him <hi type="italic">with the saving strength of his right hand;</hi> he will give a real answer to his prayers, and the prayers of his friends for him, not by letter, nor by word of mouth, but, which is much better, by his right hand, by the saving strength of his right hand. He will make it to appear that he hears him by what he does for him. <div eID="gen10701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10702" type="x-p"/> II. His people triumphing in God and their relation to him, and his revelation of himself to them, by which they distinguish themselves from those that live without God in the world. 1. See the difference between worldly people and godly people, in their confidences, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">v. 7</reference>. The children of this world trust in second causes, and think all is well if those do but smile upon them; they trust <hi type="italic">in chariots and in horses,</hi> and the more of them they can bring into the field the more sure they are of success in their wars; probably David has here an eye to the Syrians, whose forces consisted much of chariots and horsemen, as we find in the history of David's victories over them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. viii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">x. 18</reference>. "But," say the Israelites, "we neither have chariots and horses to trust to nor do we want them, nor, if we had them, would we build our hopes of success upon that; <hi type="italic">but we will remember,</hi> and rely upon, <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord our God,</hi> upon the relation we stand in to him as the Lord our God and the knowledge we have of him by his name," that is, all that whereby he makes himself known; this we will remember and upon every remembrance of it will be encouraged. Note, those who make God and his name their praise may make God and his name their trust. 2. See the difference in the issue of their confidences and by that we are to judge of the wisdom of the choice; things are as they prove; see who will be ashamed of their confidence and who not, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">v. 8</reference>. "Those that trusted in their chariots and horses are brought down and fallen, and their chariots and horses were so far from saving them that they helped to sink them, and made them the easier and the richer prey to the conqueror, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. viii. 4</reference>. But we that trust in the name of the Lord our God not only stand upright, and keep our ground, but have risen, and have got ground against the enemy, and have triumphed over them." Note, A believing obedient trust in God and his name is the surest way both to preferment and to establishment, to rise and to stand upright, and this will stand us in stead when creature-confidences fail those that depend upon them. <div eID="gen10702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10703" type="x-p"/> III. They conclude their prayer for the king with a <hi type="italic">Hosanna, "Save, now, we beseech thee,</hi> O Lord!" <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">v. 9</reference>. As we read this verse, it may be taken as a prayer that God would not only bless the king, "Save, Lord, give him success," but that he would make him a blessing to them, "<hi type="italic">Let the king hear us</hi> when we call to him for justice and mercy." Those that would have good of their magistrates must thus pray for them, for they, as all other creatures, are that to us (and no more) which God makes them to be. Or it may refer to the Messiah, that King, that King of kings; let him hear us when we call; let him come to us according to the promise, in the time appointed; let him, as the great Master of requests, receive all our petitions and present them to the Father. But many interpreters give another reading of this verse, by altering the pause, <hi type="italic">Lord, save the king, and hear us when we call;</hi> and so it is a summary of the whole psalm and is taken into our English Liturgy; <hi type="italic">O Lord! save the king, and mercifully hear us when we call upon thee.</hi> <div eID="gen10703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10704" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6-Ps.20.9">these verses</reference> we should encourage ourselves to trust in God, and stir up ourselves to pray earnestly, as we are in duty bound, for those in authority over us, that under them we may lead quiet and peaceable lives in all godliness and honesty.  <chapter eID="Ps.20"/> <div eID="gen10704" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f8a8f24d69e884a44341f41a18d0d802d3c0d78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5657"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 20</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference>. David probably composed this Psalm to express the prayers of the pious for his success as at once the head of the Church and nation. Like other compositions of which David in such relations is the subject, its sentiments have a permanent value--the prosperity of Christ's kingdom being involved, as well as typified, in that of Israel and its king.</title> <div sID="gen8603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5657"/><hi type="bold">1. hear thee--</hi>graciously (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen8603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name of--</hi>or manifested perfections, as power, wisdom, &c.<div eID="gen8604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defend thee--</hi>set thee on high from danger (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">18:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8605" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bce9e982f2df14a46222e5f1c49cb8c93887b5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5658"/><div sID="gen8606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5658"/><hi type="bold">2. strengthen thee--</hi>sustain in conflict; even physical benefits may be included, as courage for war, &c., as such may proceed from a sense of divine favor, secured in the use of spiritual privileges. <div eID="gen8606" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc8bdb6e52842d2e2c786bb7ff2a848904cccb90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5659"/><div sID="gen8607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5659"/><hi type="bold">3. all thy offerings--</hi>or gifts, vegetable offerings.<div eID="gen8607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accept--</hi>literally, "turn to ashes" (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.38">1Ki 18:38</reference>).<div eID="gen8608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Selah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Psa 3:2</reference>). <div eID="gen8609" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5c560dbfef31312dc2fb153f5799bc952734057: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5660"/><div sID="gen8610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5660"/><hi type="bold">4. thy counsel--</hi>or plan. <div eID="gen8610" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a46cc5790c16a8e22fb968a0d9989917d084d78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5661"/><div sID="gen8611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5661"/><hi type="bold">5. salvation--</hi>that wrought and experienced by him.<div eID="gen8611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set up our banners--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.2.3">Nu 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>). In usual sense, or, as some render, "may we be made great." <div eID="gen8612" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bb8b5b6b2052193f0f82891b0be1da5c4301056: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5662"/><div sID="gen8613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5662"/>6. He speaks as if suddenly assured of a hearing.<div eID="gen8613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his anointed--</hi>not only David personally, but as the specially appointed head of His Church.<div eID="gen8614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his holy heaven--</hi>or, literally, "the heavens of His holiness," where He resides (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">11:4</reference>).<div eID="gen8615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saving ... hand--</hi>His power which brings salvation. <div eID="gen8616" type="x-p"/>
entries.d08d8d6774007bac44faee6491b7513b1e573b98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5663"/><div sID="gen8617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5663"/><hi type="bold">7. remember--</hi>or cause to remember, mention thankfully (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45">1Sa 17:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16">Psa 33:16</reference>). <div eID="gen8617" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf19d889b4bfddf63e0839da8f23ce525ab24a22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5664"/><div sID="gen8618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5664"/><hi type="bold">8. They--</hi>that is, who trust in horses, &c.<div eID="gen8618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand upright--</hi>literally, "we have straightened ourselves up from our distress and fears." <div eID="gen8619" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2f349b078c032d2e5ee044e91fe628ae19eccb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5665"/><div sID="gen8620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5665"/><hi type="bold">9. let the king hear--</hi>as God's representative, delivered to deliver. Perhaps a better sense is, "Lord, save the king; hear us when we call," or pray. <chapter eID="Ps.20"/>

entries.9daf1f7fd369ecbaee4cc2d586ef39c75c04984b: <div eID="gen19128" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19129" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19130" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19130" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19129" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19131" type="x-p"/> A prayer for the king in his enterprises, that his prayers may be heard, his offerings accepted, and his wishes fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Psa.20.1-Psa.20.4">Psa 20:1-4</reference>. Confidence of victory expressed, <reference osisRef="Psa.20.5">Psa 20:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>. Vain hopes exposed; and supplication made for the king, <reference osisRef="Psa.20.7-Psa.20.9">Psa 20:7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen19131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19132" type="x-p"/> It is most likely that this Psalm was penned on the occasion of David's going to war, and most probably with the Ammonites and Syrians, who came with great numbers of horses and chariots to fight with him. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6-2Sam.10.8">2Sam 10:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Chr 19:7</reference>. It is one of the Dialogue Psalms, and appears to be thus divided: Previously to his undertaking the war, David comes to the tabernacle to offer sacrifice. This being done, the people, in the king's behalf, offer up their prayers; these are included in the three first verses: the fourth was probably spoken by the high priest; the fifth, by David and his attendants; the last clause, by the high priest; the sixth, by the high priest, after the victim was consumed; the seventh and eighth, by David and his men; and the ninth, as a chorus by all the congregation. <div eID="gen19132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19133" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19134" type="x-p"/> The Lord hear thee - David had already offered the sacrifice and prayed. The people implore God to succor him in the day of trouble; of both personal and national danger. <div eID="gen19134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19135" type="x-p"/> The name of the God of Jacob - This refers to Jacob's wrestling with the Angel; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen 32:24</reference> (note), etc. And who was this Angel? Evidently none other than the Angel of the Covenant, the Lord Jesus, in whom was the name of God, the fullness of the Godhead bodily. He was the God of Jacob, who blessed Jacob, and gave him a new name and a new nature. See the notes on the above place in Genesis.
entries.13535a29b903c3f4ff55b5aa0d4f7d2fd45b4f06: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19136" type="x-p"/> Send thee help from the sanctuary - This was the place where God recorded his name; the place where he was to be sought, and the place where he manifested himself. He dwelt between the cherubim over the mercyseat. He is now in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. This is the true sanctuary where God must be sought. <div eID="gen19136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19137" type="x-p"/> Strengthen thee out of Zion - The temple or tabernacle where his prayers and sacrifices were to be offered.
entries.a2fd406e10405517d237407dfb904f548384fdcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19138" type="x-p"/> Remember all thy offerings - The minchah, which is here mentioned, was a gratitude-offering. It is rarely used to signify a bloody sacrifice. <div eID="gen19138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19139" type="x-p"/> Burnt sacrifice - The olah here mentioned was a bloody sacrifice. The blood of the victim was spilt at the altar, and the flesh consumed. One of these offerings implied a consciousness of sin in the offerer; and this sacrifice he brought as an atonement: the other implied a sense of mercies already received, and was offered in the way of gratitude. <div eID="gen19139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19140" type="x-p"/> David presents himself before the Lord with offerings of both kinds. <div eID="gen19140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19141" type="x-p"/> This prayer of the people is concluded with Selah, which we have taken up in the general sense of so be it. Hear and answer. It will and must be so, etc.
entries.8b57e1d5af5fa076f17100c3fea5659883ea6544: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19142" type="x-p"/> Grant thee according to thine own heart - May God give thee whatsoever thou art setting thy heart upon, and accomplish all thy desires! This was probably the prayer of the high priest.
entries.7b4af5c9611ceb464b6aa2255625ee751108758e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19143" type="x-p"/> We will rejoice in thy salvation - We expect help from thee alone; it is in thy cause we engage; and to thee, as our war is a just one, we consecrate our banners, inscribed with thy name. It is said that the Maccabees had their name from the inscription on their banners; which was taken from <reference osisRef="Exo.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>, מי כמכה באלם יהוה mi camochah baelim Yehovah, "Who is like unto thee, O Lord, among the gods?" The word being formed from the initial letters מ M, כ C, ב B, י I, מכבי Ma Ca B I, whence Maccabeus and Maccabees. <div eID="gen19143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19144" type="x-p"/> The words of this verse were spoken by David and his officers; immediately after which I suppose the high priest to have added, The Lord fulfill all thy petitions!
entries.2bfa53e00e523ac2fc4bbe707bfb087548480723: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19145" type="x-p"/> Now know I that the Lord saveth his anointed - These are probably the words of the priest after the victim had been consumed; and those signs had accompanied the offering, which were proofs of God's acceptance of the sacrifice; and, consequently, that the campaign would have a successful issue. David is God's anointed; therefore, he is under his especial care. He will hear him. David must continue to pray, and to depend on God; else he cannot expect continual salvation. David has vast multitudes of enemies against him; he, therefore, requires supernatural help. Because of this, God will hear him with the saving strength of his right hand. <div eID="gen19145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19146" type="x-p"/> The Hand of God is his power, the Right hand, his almighty power; the Strength of his right hand, his almighty power in action; the Saving strength of his right hand, the miraculous effects wrought by his almighty power brought into action. This is what David was to expect; and it was the prospect of this that caused him and his officers to exult as they do in the following verse.
entries.893bf87292f5d56ad8ac5fa23b0c1ee3286654be: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19147" type="x-p"/> Some trust in chariots - The words of the original are short and emphatic: These in chariots; and these in horses; but we will record in the name of Jehovah our God. Or, as the Septuagint, μεγαλυνθησομεθα, "we shall be magnified." Or, as the Vulgate, invocabimus, "we shall invoke the name of the Lord." This and the following verse I suppose to be the words of David and his officers. And the mention of chariots and horses makes it likely that the war with the Ammonites and Syrians is that to which reference is made here; for they came against him with vast multitudes of horsemen and chariots. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6-2Sam.10.8">2Sam 10:6-8</reference>. According to the law, David could neither have chariots nor horses; and those who came against him with cavalry must have a very great advantage; but he saw that Jehovah his God was more than a match for all his foes, and in him he trusts with implicit confidence.
entries.fac9b874140417a82fd03146ddb6e5404c99c980: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19148" type="x-p"/> They are brought down and fallen - They were so confident of victory that they looked upon it as already gained. They who trusted in their horses and chariots are bowed down, and prostrated on the earth: they are all overthrown. <div eID="gen19148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19149" type="x-p"/> But we are risen - We who have trusted in the name of Jehovah are raised up from all despondency; and we stand upright - we shall conquer, and go on to conquer.
entries.92c56a78a9845dccc09f3eece2f67e468e1a90b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19150" type="x-p"/> Save, Lord - This verse was spoken by all the congregation, and was the chorus and conclusion of the piece. <div eID="gen19150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19151" type="x-p"/> The verse may be read, Lord, save the king! He will hear as in the day of our calling. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, Anglo-Saxon, read the verse thus: Lord, save the king! and hear us whensoever we shall call upon thee. The Syriac reads differently: The Lord will save us: and our king will hear us in the day in which we shall call upon him. This refers all to God: while the others refer the latter clause to David. Lord, save David; and David will save us. "If thou preservest him, he will be thy minister for good to us." This appears to be the easiest sense of the place, and harmonizes with all the rest.  <chapter eID="Ps.20"/> <div eID="gen19151" type="x-p"/>

entries.f321234082d5a79ccc5a3a6bff5433e4d1ce033a: <div eID="gen9258" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer for the King in Time of War</title> <div sID="gen9259" type="x-p"/> To <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> is closely attached <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference>, because its commencement is as it were the echo of the prayer with which the former closes; and to <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference> is closely attached <reference osisRef="Ps.21.1-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:1-13</reference>, because both Psalms refer to the same event relatively, as prayer and thanksgiving. <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference> is an intercessory psalm of the nation, and <reference osisRef="Ps.21.1-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:1-13</reference> a thanksgiving psalm of the nation, on behalf of its king. It is clearly manifest that the two Psalms form a pair, being connected by unity of author and subject. They both open somewhat uniformly with a synonymous parallelism of the members, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2-Ps.20.6">Psa 20:2-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2-Ps.21.8">Psa 21:2-8</reference>; they then increase in fervour and assume a more vivid colouring as they come to speak of the foes of the king and the empire, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:9-13</reference>; and they both close with an ejaculatory cry to Jahve, Ps 20:10; 21:14. In both, the king is apostrophised through the course of the several verses, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2-Ps.20.6">Psa 20:2-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:9-13</reference>; and here and there this is done in a way that provokes the question whether the words are not rather addressed to Jahve, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>; Psa 21:10. In both Psalms the king is referred to by המּלך, Ps 20:10; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.8">Psa 21:8</reference>; both comprehend the goal of the desires in the word ישׁוּעה, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2">Psa 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.6">Psa 21:6</reference>; both delight in rare forms of expression, which are found only in these instances in the whole range of Old Testament literature, viz., נדגל <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>, נתעדד <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference>, ארשׁת <reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>, תחדהו, Psa 21:7. <div eID="gen9259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9260" type="x-p"/> If, as the לדוד indicates, they formed part of the oldest Davidic Psalter, then it is notwithstanding more probable that their author is a contemporary poet, than that it is David himself. For, although both as to form of expression (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.12">Psa 21:12</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>) and as to thoughts (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.7">Psa 21:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>), they exhibit some points of contact with Davidic Psalms, they still stand isolated by their peculiar character. But that David is their subject, as the inscription לדוד, and their position in the midst of the Davidic Psalms, lead one to expect, is capable of confirmation. During the time of the Syro-Ammonitish war comes David’s deep fall, which in itself and in its consequences made him sick both in soul and in body. It was not until he was again restored to God’s favour out of this self-incurred peril, that he went to his army which lay before Rabbath Ammon, and completed the conquest of the royal city of the enemy. The most satisfactory explanation of the situation referred to in this couplet of Psalms is to be gained from 2 Sam 11-12. <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference> prays for the recovery of the king, who is involved in war with powerful foes; and <reference osisRef="Ps.21.1-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:1-13</reference> gives thanks for his recovery, and wishes him a victorious issue to the approaching campaign. The “chariots and horses” (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference>) are characteristic of the military power of Aram (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference>, and frequently), and in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Psa 21:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.21.10">Psa 21:10</reference> we perceive an allusion to <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30-2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:30-31</reference>, or at least a remarkable agreement with what is there recorded.
entries.2742f1cdd498ce7d5136789176b87827cd20e83f: <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.5">Psa 20:1-5</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_20:2-6) Litany for the king in distress, who offers sacrifices for himself in the sanctuary. The futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2">Psa 20:2</reference>, standing five times at the head of the climactic members of the parallelism, are optatives. ימלּא, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>, also continues the chain of wishes, of which even נרננה (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.15">Psa 69:15</reference>) forms one of the links. The wishes of the people accompany both the prayer and the sacrifice. “The Name of the God of Jacob” is the self-manifesting power and grace of the God of Israel. יעקב is used in poetry interchangeably with ישראל, just like אלהים with יהוה. Alshêch refers to <reference osisRef="Gen.35.3">Gen 35:3</reference>; and it is not improbable that the desire moulds itself after the fashion of the record of the fact there handed down to us. May Jahve, who, as the history of Jacob shows, hears (and answers) in the day of distress, hear the king; may the Name of the God of Jacob bear him away from his foes to a triumphant height. שׂגּב alternates with רומם (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.49">Psa 18:49</reference>) in this sense. This intercession on the behalf of the praying one is made in the sanctuary on the heights of Zion, where Jahve sits enthroned. May He send him succour from thence, like auxiliary troops that decide the victory. The king offers sacrifice. He offers sacrifice according to custom before the commencement of the battle (1Sa 13:9., and cf. the phrase קדּשׁ מלחמה), a whole burnt-offering and at the same time a meat or rather meal offering also, מנחות;<note placement="foot">This, though not occurring in the Old Testament, is the principal form of the plural, which, as even David Kimchi recognises in his <hi type="italic">Lexicon</hi>, points to a verb מנח (just as שׂמלות, גּבעות, שׁפחות point to שׂמל, גּבע, שׂפח); whereas other old grammarians supposed נחה to be the root, and were puzzled with the traditional pronunciation <hi type="italic">menachôth</hi>, but without reason.</note> for every whole offering and every <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> - or peace-offering had a meat-offering and a drink-offering as its indispensable accompaniment. The word זכר is perfectly familiar in the ritual of the meal-offering. That portion of the meal-offering, only a part of which was placed upon the altar (to which, however, according to traditional practice, does not belong the accompanying meal-offering of the מנחת נסכים, which was entirely devoted to the altar), which ascended with the altar fire is called אזכּרה, μνημόσυνον (cf. <reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">Act 10:4</reference>), that which brings to remembrance with God him for whom it is offered up (not “incense,” as Hupfeld renders it); for the designation of the offering of jealousy, Num 5:15, as “bringing iniquity to remembrance before God” shows, that in the meal-offering ritual זכר retains the very same meaning that it has in other instances. Every meal-offering is in a certain sense a מנחת זכּרון a esnes . Hence here the prayer that Jahve would graciously remember them is combined with the meal-offerings. <div eID="gen9260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9261" type="x-p"/> As regards the <hi type="italic">‛olah</hi>, the wish “let fire from heaven (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Lev 9:24</reference>; 1Ki 18:38; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.26">1Ch 21:26</reference>) turn it to ashes,” would not be vain. But the language does not refer to anything extraordinary; and in itself the consumption of the offering to ashes (Böttcher) is no mark of gracious acceptance. Moreover, as a denominative from דּשׁן, fat ashes, דּשּׁן means “to clean from ashes,” and not: to turn into ashes. On the other hand, דּשּׁן also signifies “to make fat,” <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>, and this effective signification is applied declaratively in this instance: may He find thy burnt-offering fat, which is equivalent to: may it be to Him a ריח ניחח [an odour of satisfaction, a sweet-smelling savour]. The voluntative <hi type="italic">ah</hi> only occurs here and in <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference> (which see) and <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>, in the <hi type="italic">3 pers</hi>.; and in this instance, just as with the cohortative in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference>, we have a change of the lengthening into a sharpening of the sound (cf. the exactly similar change of forms in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference>; Zec 5:4; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.14">Pro 24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.13">Eze 25:13</reference>) as is very frequently the case in מה for מה. The alteration to ידשּׁנה or ידשׁנהּ (Hitzig) is a felicitous but needless way of getting rid of the rare form. The explanation of the intensifying of the music here is, that the intercessory song of the choir is to be simultaneous with the presentation upon the altar (הקטרה). עצה is the resolution formed in the present wartime. “Because of thy salvation,” i.e., thy success in war, is, as all the language is here, addressed to the king, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2">Psa 21:2</reference>, where it is addressed to Jahve, and intended of the victory accorded to him. It is needless to read נגדּל instead of נדגּל, after the rendering of the lxx megaluntheeso'metha. נדגּל is a denominative from דּגל: to wave a banner. In the closing line, the rejoicing of hope goes back again to the present and again assumes the form of an intercessory desire.
entries.a31e159b49de496de699727d6ed5b6d9fcf250c5: <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6-Ps.20.8">Psa 20:6-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_20:7-9) While <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2">Psa 20:2</reference> were being sung the offering of the sacrifice was probably going on. Now, after a lengthened pause, there ascends a voice, probably the voice of one of the Levites, expressing the cheering assurance of the gracious acceptance of the offering that has been presented by the priest. With עתּה or ועתּה, the usual word to indicate the turning-point, the instantaneous entrance of the result of some previous process of prolonged duration, whether hidden or manifest (e.g., 1Ki 17:24; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">Isa 29:22</reference>), is introduced. howshiya` is the perfect of faith, which, in the certainty of being answered, realises the fulfilment in anticipation. The exuberance of the language in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference> corresponds to the exuberance of feeling which thus finds expression. <div eID="gen9261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9262" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Psa 20:3</reference> the answer is expected out of Zion, in the present instance it is looked for from God’s holy heavens; for the God who sits enthroned in Zion is enthroned for ever in the heavens. His throne on earth is as it were the vestibule of His heavenly throne; His presence in the sanctuary of Israel is no limitation of His omnipresence; His help out of Zion is the help of the Celestial One and Him who is exalted above the heaven of heavens. גּבוּרות does not here mean the fulness of might (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Psa 90:10</reference>), but the displays of power (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.2">Psa 106:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.4">Psa 145:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.150.2">Psa 150:2</reference>; Psa 63:1-11 :15), by which His right hand procures salvation, i.e., victory, for the combatant. The glory of Israel is totally different from that of the heathen, which manifests itself in boastful talk. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference></hi> הזכּירוּ or יזכּירוּ must be supplied from the נזכּיר in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference></hi> (lxx μεγαλυνθησόμεθα = נגביר, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Psa 12:5</reference>); הזכּיר בּ, to make laudatory mention of any matter, to extol, and indirectly therefore to take credit to one’s self for it, to boast of it (cf. הלּל בּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">Psa 44:9</reference>). According to the Law Israel was forbidden to have any standing army; and the law touching the king (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">Deu 17:16</reference>) speaks strongly against his keeping many horses. It was also the same under the judges, and at this time under David; but under Solomon, who acquired for himself horses and chariots in great number (1Ki 10:26-29), it was very different. It is therefore a confession that must belong to the time of David which is here made in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference>, viz., that Israel’s glory in opposition to their enemies, especially the Syrians, is the sure defence and protection of the Name of their God alone. The language of David to Goliath is very similar, 1Sa 17:45. The preterites in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference> are <hi type="italic">praet. confidentiae</hi>. It is, as Luther says, “a song of triumph before the victory, a shout of joy before succour.” Since קוּם does not mean to stand, but to rise, קמנוּ assumes the present superiority of the enemy. But the position of affairs changes: those who stand fall, and those who are lying down rise up; the former remain lying, the latter keep the field. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התעודד signifies to show one’s self firm, strong, courageous; like עודד, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">Psa 146:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.6">Psa 147:6</reference>, to strengthen, confirm, recover, from עוּד to be compact, firm, cogn. Arab. <hi type="italic">âd</hi> <hi type="italic">f. i.</hi>, inf. <hi type="italic">aid</hi>, strength; as, e.g., the Koran (<hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. xxxviii. 16) calls David <hi type="italic">dhâ - l - aidi</hi>, possessor of strength, II <hi type="italic">ajjada</hi>, to strengthen, support, and Arab. <hi type="italic">'dd</hi>, inf. <hi type="italic">add</hi>, strength superiority, V <hi type="italic">tāddada</hi>, to show one’s self strong, brave, courageous.
entries.c898d65342d159aa7c2003e78f782aaa087d02e5: <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_v. 10) After this solo voice, the chorus again come on. The song is closed, as it was opened, by the whole congregation; and is rounded off by recurring to its primary note, praying for the accomplishment of that which is sought and pledged. The accentuation construes המּלך with יעננוּ as its subject, perhaps in consideration of the fact, that הושׁיעה is not usually followed by a governed object, and because thus a medium is furnished for the transition from address to direct assertion. But if in a Psalm, the express object of which is to supplicate salvation for the king, המלך הושׁיעה stand side by side, then, in accordance with the connection, המלך must be treated as the object; and more especially since Jahve is called מלך רב, in <reference osisRef="Ps.48.3">Psa 48:3</reference>, and the like, but never absolutely המלך. Wherefore it is, with Hupfeld, Hitzig, and others, to be rendered according to the lxx and Vulgate, <hi type="italic">Domine salvum fac regem</hi>. The New Testament cry Ὡσαννὰ τῷ υἱῷ Δαυίδ is a peculiar application of this Davidic “God bless the king (God save the king),” which is brought about by means of Psa 118:25. The closing line, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference></hi>, is an expanded Amen.  <chapter eID="Ps.20"/> <div eID="gen9262" type="x-p"/>

entries.c9cf9a0ffe36faf6dc3305224075270311a25810:
PSALM 20.
This psalm contains a common prayer of the Church in behalf of the King of Israel, that God would succor him in danger; and in behalf of his kingdom, that God would maintain it in safety, and cause it to prosper: for in the person of David the safety and well-being of the whole community centred. To this there is added a promise, that God will preside over that kingdom of which he was the founder, and so effectually watch over it as to secure its continual preservation.
To the chief musician. A Psalm of David.
Psalm 20:1-2
1. May Jehovah hear thee in the day of trouble! may the name of the God of Jacob defend thee! 2. May he send thee help from his sanctuary, and sustain thee out of Sion!
 
The inscription shows that the psalm was composed by David; but though he was its author, there is no absurdity in his speaking of himself in the person of others. The office of a prophet having been committed to him, he with great propriety prepared this as a form of prayer for the use of the faithful. In doing this, his object was not so much to commend his own person, by authoritatively issuing a royal ordinance enjoining upon the people the use of this prayer, as to show, in the exercise of his office as a teacher, that it belonged to the whole Church to concern itself, and to use its endeavors that the kingdom which God had erected might continue safe and prosperous. Many interpreters view this prayer as offered up only on one particular occasion; but in this I cannot agree. The occasion of its composition at first may have arisen from some particular battle which was about to be fought, either against the Ammonites, or against some other enemies of Israel. But the design of the Holy Spirit, in my judgment, was to deliver to the Church a common form of prayer, which, as we may gather from the words, was to be used whenever she was threatened with any danger. God commands his people, in general, to pray for kings, but there was a special reason, and one which did not apply to any other kingdom, why prayer was to be made in behalf of this kingdom; for it was only by the hand of David and his seed that God had determined to govern and maintain his people. It is particularly to be noticed, that under the figure of this temporal kingdom, there was described a government far more excellent, on which the whole joy and felicity of the Church depended. The object, therefore, which David had expressly in view was, to exhort all the children of God to cherish such a holy solicitude about the kingdom of Christ, as would stir them up to continual prayer in its behalf.
1. May Jehovah hear thee, etc. The Holy Spirit, by introducing the people as praying that God would answer the prayers of the king, is to be viewed as at the same time admonishing kings that it is their duty to implore the protection of God in all their affairs. When he says, In the day of trouble, he shows that they will not be exempted from troubles, and he does this that they may not become discouraged, if at any time they should happen to be in circumstances of danger. In short, the faithful, that the body may not be separated from the head, further the king’s prayers by their common and united supplications. The name of God is here put for God himself and not without good reason; for the essence of God being incomprehensible to us, it behoves us to trust in him, in so far as his grace and power are made known to us. From his name, therefore, proceeds confidence in calling upon him. The faithful desire that the king may be protected and aided by God, whose name was called upon among the sons of Jacob. I cannot agree with those who think that mention is here made of that patriarch, because God exercised him with various afflictions, not unlike those with which he tried his servant David. I am rather of opinion that, as is usual in Scripture, the chosen people are denoted by the term Jacob. And from this name, the God of Jacob, the faithful encourage themselves to pray for the defense of their king; because it was one of the privileges of their adoption to live under the conduct and protection of a king set over them by God himself. Hence we may conclude, as I have said before, that under the figure of a temporal kingdom there is described to us a government much more excellent.
“Et de le il nous convient recueiller, ce que jay dit, que sous a figure d’un regne temporel nous est descrie un gouvernement bien plus excellent.” — Fr.
Since Christ our King, being an everlasting priest, never ceases to make intercession with God, the whole body of the Church should unite in prayer with him;
As the people of Israel here unite in prayer with and for the monarch of Israel, whom we may picture to our minds as repairing to the tabernacle to offer sacrifices, where this animated ode was sung by the priests and people.
and farther, we can have no hope of being heard except he go before us, and conduct us to God.
“Si non qu’il marche derant, et nous conduise a Dieu.” — Fr.
And it serves in no small degree to assuage our sorrows to consider that Jesus Christ, when we are afflicted, accounts our distresses his own, provided we, at the same time, take courage, and continue resolute and magnanimous in tribulation; which we should be prepared to do, since the Holy Spirit here forewarns us that the kingdom of Christ would be subject to dangers and troubles.

                     <ns0:head>The ARGUMENT.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> contains a Prayer to be used by the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, both now on the behalf of King <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> when he was undertaking some great Expedition, going forth, as is supposed, against the <ns0:hi>Ammonites,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Syrians, 2 Sam. 10.</ns0:hi> or some other potent Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies, and hereafter in like Cases.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:head>To the chief musician, <ns0:hi>a Psalm</ns0:hi> of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THe LORD hear thee in the day of trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In this time of War and Danger.</ns0:note>: the Name of the God of <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi>) God himself; For <ns0:hi>Names</ns0:hi> are oft put for Persons, as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 26. 53. <ns0:hi>A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 1. 15. and 4. 12. and <ns0:hi>the Name of God,</ns0:hi> for God, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 58. <ns0:hi>Ne<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
